lessons.title: Siting and Constructing a Farm Pond
lessons.body:
A farm pond is a hole in the ground that catches and holds water for irrigation. You want to build it where water naturally collects, like at the bottom of a slope or where two gullies meet. Avoid steep slopes unless you plan to build a dam. The pond should be at least 2 meters deep so it doesn't dry out quickly. If your soil is sandy, water will drain away; you need clay soil or you must line the pond with a thick layer of clay or a plastic liner. Test by digging a small hole, filling it with water, and seeing if it holds overnight.

To construct, mark the area with stakes and string. Dig with a hoe, shovel, and pickaxe. Make the sides slope gently (about 1 meter horizontal for every 1 meter vertical) so they don't collapse. Pile the excavated soil around the edges to form a berm (a raised bank) to stop runoff from flowing in and to increase depth. The inlet should be a shallow channel that leads water from a higher area. Install a simple silt trap: a small pit before the inlet where sand and debris settle. This keeps the pond from filling with mud.

Line the pond bottom and sides with clay if needed. Spread 30 cm of clay, wet it, and compact it by walking or tamping. Alternatively, use a 1 mm thick UV-resistant plastic liner, but this is expensive and can tear. A cheaper method is to use a mixture of clay and cow dung, which seals cracks. After filling, add a few buckets of manure tea to encourage algae, which seals tiny leaks.

Maintain your pond by checking for leaks, clearing silt from the inlet, and keeping animals away from the banks. A well-built pond of 10m x 10m x 2m deep holds about 200,000 liters, enough to irrigate a quarter-hectare of vegetables for a month. Use a bucket and rope, or a small pump, to get water out. Never let the pond dry completely; keep at least 30 cm of water to protect the liner and seal.

lessons.title: Rainwater Harvesting: Gutters, Tanks, and Cisterns
lessons.body:
Rainwater harvesting means catching rain from roofs and storing it for dry spells. A typical iron sheet roof of 50 square meters can collect 500 liters from just 10 mm of rain. To calculate your potential: roof area (mÂ²) x rainfall (mm) x 0.8 (efficiency) = liters. For example, 50 mÂ² x 800 mm annual rain x 0.8 = 32,000 liters per year. That's enough to irrigate a small garden.

Start with gutters. Use PVC pipes cut in half, or buy ready-made gutters. Slope them 1 cm for every 3 meters toward the tank. Install a first-flush diverter: a small pipe that dumps the first 20 liters of rain, which carries dirt and bird droppings. Use a mesh screen over the gutter to keep out leaves. For tanks, you can use plastic drums (200 liters), ferrocement tanks (1,000â5,000 liters), or underground cisterns. Ferrocement is cheap: build a wire mesh frame, plaster with cement-sand mix (1:3), and cure for 7 days. A 2,000-liter tank costs about $50 in materials.

Place tanks on a raised platform (at least 1 meter) so you can gravity-feed water to your garden. Connect a tap near the bottom. For underground cisterns, dig a pit, line with bricks or concrete, and cover with a strong lid. Cisterns keep water cool and reduce evaporation, but you need a pump to get water out.

Keep water clean: cover tanks to stop mosquitoes and algae, and clean gutters before the rainy season. Use a cloth filter over the tank inlet. Test water for contamination if you plan to drink it, but for irrigation it's usually fine. A 5,000-liter tank can irrigate 100 tomato plants for two weeks. Always store more than you think you need; a dry year can cut rainfall by half.

lessons.title: Drilling and Maintaining a Shallow Well
lessons.body:
A shallow well is a hole dug or drilled to reach groundwater, usually less than 15 meters deep. It's the cheapest way to get water if you have a high water table. First, find a spot where the ground stays damp, or where plants grow greener in the dry season. You can also use a water diviner, but a simple test is to dig a small hole 1 meter deep and see if it fills with water overnight.

To dig by hand, use a shovel, pickaxe, and bucket. Dig a circular hole about 1.2 meters wide. As you go deeper, line the walls with concrete rings or bricks to prevent collapse. Lower the rings as you dig. Stop when you hit a layer of sand or gravel that fills with water. The water should seep in from the bottom. If the hole stays dry, dig deeper or try another spot. For a drilled well, hire a manual drilling rig (like a hand auger) or a small machine. A 10 cm diameter PVC pipe with slots at the bottom is driven into the ground. This is faster but needs equipment.

After drilling, install a pump. A hand pump (like the India Mark II) is reliable and cheap. For irrigation, use a small submersible pump (0.5â1 HP) powered by solar panels or a generator. A 1 HP pump can lift 1,000 liters per hour from 10 meters. Place the pump intake 1 meter above the bottom to avoid sucking mud.

Maintain your well by keeping animals and dirty buckets away. Seal the top with a concrete slab and a removable lid. Check the pump seals every 3 months. If water becomes cloudy or smells, shock-chlorinate: pour 1 liter of bleach (5% chlorine) into the well, wait 12 hours, then pump out until clear. Never let the well run dry; it can burn out the pump. A well yielding 500 liters per hour can irrigate 0.2 hectares of maize.

lessons.title: Using Streams and Canals with Small Pumps
lessons.body:
Streams and canals are free water sources, but you need a pump to lift water to your field. First, measure the flow: use a bucket and stopwatch. If a 10-liter bucket fills in 5 seconds, that's 2 liters per second, or 7,200 liters per hour. That's plenty for a small pump. Check the drop (head) from the water surface to your highest point. A pump must overcome both height and friction in the pipe. For every 10 meters of horizontal pipe, add 1 meter of head. So if you lift 5 meters and pipe 30 meters, total head is 8 meters.

Choose a pump. For smallholders, a 1-inch or 2-inch centrifugal pump (1â2 HP) is common. Petrol pumps are powerful but costly to run; solar pumps are cheaper long-term. A 1 HP petrol pump can move 10,000 liters per hour at 10 meters head. Use a suction hose with a strainer on the end to keep out debris. Place the pump as close to the water as possible, and prime it (fill with water) before starting.

For canals, you may need a permit from local authorities. Never block the canal completely; leave a gate to release water. Build a small dam or weir to create a pool for the pump intake. Use sandbags or rocks. If the stream is far, dig a furrow or lay a pipe to your field. A 50 mm diameter pipe can carry 5,000 liters per hour with a 1-meter drop.

Maintain your pump: clean the air filter, change oil every 50 hours, and check for leaks. In the dry season, streams may drop. Dig a sump (a small hole) in the stream bed to collect water. Never pump muddy water; it wears out the impeller. Store your pump in a dry place. A well-maintained pump lasts 5 years. With a 2 HP pump, you can irrigate 1 hectare of rice from a stream.

lessons.title: Water Storage Options: Tanks, Reservoirs, and Dams
lessons.body:
Storing water lets you irrigate during dry spells. The three main options are tanks, reservoirs, and dams. Tanks are small (200â10,000 liters) and made of plastic, metal, or ferrocement. They are good for household use and small gardens. A 5,000-liter tank costs $100â$300. Place it on a stand 2 meters high for gravity flow. Plastic tanks are easy to move but degrade in sunlight; paint them or cover with shade. Metal tanks rust; line with food-grade plastic. Ferrocement tanks are cheapest for large volumes: build a wire frame, plaster with cement, and cure. They last 20 years.

Reservoirs are larger, often lined ponds or excavated tanks. A reservoir of 100,000 liters can be a lined pit 10m x 10m x 1m deep. Line with clay, plastic, or concrete. Reservoirs are good for storing rainwater or pumped water. They lose water to evaporation and seepage. Cover with a floating cover or shade net to reduce evaporation by 80%. Add a silt trap before the reservoir.

Dams are built across streams or valleys. A small earth dam is a wall of compacted soil with a clay core. It must have a spillway (a wide channel) to let excess water pass safely. A dam 3 meters high and 20 meters long can store 1 million liters. You need a permit and engineering advice. Dams are expensive ($1,000â$5,000) but store huge volumes. Build during the dry season. Use a bulldozer or manual labor. Key: compact soil in 20 cm layers, and keep the dam wall dry on the downstream side.

For all storage, prevent evaporation and contamination. Cover tanks, fence reservoirs, and keep animals out. Check for leaks monthly. A 10,000-liter tank can irrigate 0.1 hectare of vegetables for a week. Always store more than you need; a dry year can cut rainfall by half.

lessons.title: Protecting Water Quality from Contamination
lessons.body:
Clean water is essential for healthy crops and people. Contamination comes from animals, human waste, chemicals, and soil. Protect your water source by keeping animals at least 30 meters away. Build a fence around wells and ponds. For wells, seal the top with a concrete slab and a tight lid. Never use a dirty bucket; use a dedicated rope and bucket. For rainwater, install a first-flush diverter and clean gutters before the rainy season. Cover tanks to keep out leaves, insects, and rats.

Test your water. You can buy a simple test kit for $10â$20 that checks for bacteria (E. coli) and nitrates. If you don't have a kit, look for signs: cloudy water, bad smell, or algae. For irrigation, some contamination is okay, but for drinking, it must be clean. If water is contaminated, treat it. Boiling kills bacteria but uses fuel. Chlorination: add 2 drops of unscented bleach (5% chlorine) per liter, wait 30 minutes. For large tanks, use 1 liter of bleach per 1,000 liters. Let it sit overnight, then test for chlorine smell. If it smells, it's safe.

Prevent chemical contamination. Never mix pesticides near water sources. Store chemicals in a locked shed, away from wells. Use organic fertilizers like compost instead of raw manure, which can carry E. coli. If you use manure, compost it for at least 6 months before applying. Keep runoff from animal pens away from ponds; dig a diversion ditch.

Maintain water quality by cleaning tanks every 6 months. Drain, scrub with a brush and mild bleach solution, rinse well. For ponds, remove debris and control algae with barley straw (a small bale per 100 mÂ²). If you see dead fish or frogs, test for pollution. A clean water source means fewer diseases and better crop yields. Always store water in a covered container, and use a filter (cloth or ceramic) before drinking.

lessons.title: Practical Reference
lessons.body:
Practical Reference: Water Sources and Storage for Smallholder Irrigation

Water is the single largest determinant of whether a smallholder irrigation enterprise succeeds or fails. In sub-Saharan Africa, where 95% of agriculture is rain-fed but rainfall is increasingly erratic, the ability to capture, store, and protect water during dry spells is what separates a subsistence plot from a commercial operation. This practical reference consolidates the technical essentials of siting ponds, harvesting rainwater, drilling shallow wells, pumping from streams, storing water at scale, and safeguarding quality â all framed around the business case for each intervention.

Before investing in any structure, calculate your crop water requirement. A general rule: a 1-hectare vegetable plot in a semi-arid African climate needs roughly 4,000â6,000 mÂ³ per season. Your water source and storage must match this figure, or your enterprise will collapse in the first dry spell.

1. Siting and Constructing a Farm Pond

A farm pond is the cheapest bulk storage option for a smallholder. Site it at the lowest point of your plot where runoff naturally collects, but at least 30 m downhill from latrines, livestock pens, and chemical stores. The pond should be 30â50 mÂ³ for a 0.25 ha vegetable plot, with a depth of 2.5â3 m to reduce evaporation losses (evaporation in African savanna climates can reach 2,000 mm/year). Line the bottom and sides with compacted clay (30 cm) or a 1.5 mm HDPE geomembrane if the soil is sandy. Include a silt trap and a spillway to prevent overflow erosion. A well-built pond pays for itself in one season of dry-spell irrigation.

2. Rainwater Harvesting: Gutters, Tanks, and Cisterns

Roof catchment is the highest-quality water on the farm. A 100 mÂ² iron-sheet roof in a 700 mm rainfall zone yields roughly 70,000 L per year â enough to irrigate 0.1 ha of high-value vegetables through a dry spell. Use 110 mm PVC gutters with a first-flush diverter (discard the first 20â25 L to remove bird droppings and dust). Store in food-grade polyethylene tanks (1,000â10,000 L) or underground ferrocement cisterns. Underground cisterns cost more upfront but reduce evaporation and algae growth. For business viability, target high-value crops (tomatoes, peppers, herbs) that generate KES 200,000+ per hectare under irrigation.

3. Drilling and Maintaining a Shallow Well

Shallow wells (8â20 m) tap the top of the water table and are ideal where the water table is within 15 m of the surface. Hand-augering costs a fraction of machine drilling and can be done by trained local artisans. Install a 150 mm PVC casing with slotted screen at the bottom, a gravel pack, and a sanitary seal at the top to prevent surface contamination. Test yield with a bailer before committing to a pump. Maintain by annual chlorination, cleaning the apron, and inspecting the pump seals. A shallow well with a solar pump can irrigate 0.2â0.5 ha year-round.

4. Using Streams and Canals with Small Pumps

Streams and canals provide consistent flow but require pumping. For smallholders, petrol-powered centrifugal pumps (2â5 HP) are affordable but costly to run (fuel can consume 30â40% of gross margin). Solar surface pumps (300â1,500 W) have higher upfront cost but near-zero operating cost and a 5â10 year payback. Position the intake upstream of livestock crossings and settlements, use a sand filter before the pump, and never pump more than 30% of dry-season flow â both for ecological and legal reasons.

5. Water Storage Options: Tanks, Reservoirs, and Dams

Storage decouples water availability from irrigation timing â the core of commercial reliability. Compare options in the table below. For most smallholders, a combination of a 10,000 L tank for clean water and a 50 mÂ³ pond for bulk irrigation gives the best return.

Table 1: Cost and performance comparison of smallholder water storage options (Kenya, 2023 estimates)
Storage TypeCapacityUpfront Cost (USD)Cost per mÂ³ storedLifespanBest Use
Poly tank (above ground)5,000 L450â70090â14010â15 yrsClean water, drip irrigation
Ferrocement cistern10,000 L600â90060â9020+ yrsUnderground, low evaporation
Lined farm pond50 mÂ³800â1,50016â305â10 yrs (liner)Bulk irrigation
Earthen dam/reservoir500 mÂ³4,000â8,0008â1615â25 yrsCommunity/multi-farm
Shallow well + tank10,000 L buffer1,200â2,500â15+ yrsYear-round supply

Source: Compiled from FAO AQUASTAT country data (2020) and SNV Kenya smallholder irrigation cost surveys (2022).

6. Protecting Water Quality from Contamination

Contaminated irrigation water destroys market access â buyers reject produce with faecal contamination, and WHO/FAO guidelines set E. coli limits for fresh vegetables. Protect your investment with these measures:

â  SAFETY WARNING â Contamination Risk

Never site a well, pond, or tank within 30 m downhill of a pit latrine, septic tank, animal pen, or chemical store. A single contaminated well can cause cholera or typhoid in your household and destroy your farm's market certification. Always use a first-flush diverter on roof catchment, keep all storage covered, and chlorinate wells annually. If you suspect contamination, stop irrigation immediately and test the water before resuming. In areas with schistosomiasis, avoid wading in ponds and canals.

Table 2: Water quality parameters and smallholder management actions
ParameterSafe Level for IrrigationRisk if ExceededManagement Action
E. coli< 100 CFU/100 mLCrop contamination, illnessCover storage, chlorinate, first-flush diverter
Salinity (EC)< 2 dS/mYield loss, soil salinisationLeach with fresh water, choose salt-tolerant crops
Sediment/turbidity< 50 NTUClogged drip emittersSand filter, silt trap, settling pond
Nitrate< 30 mg/LExcess vegetative growthReduce fertiliser near water source
Pesticide residueBelow MRLMarket rejectionBuffer zones, no spraying near water

Source: FAO, Water Quality for Agriculture (Irrigation and Drainage Paper 29 Rev. 1, 1985); WHO Guidelines for the Safe Use of Wastewater in Agriculture (2006).

Quick Reference Checklist

  1. Calculate crop water requirement (mÂ³/season) before choosing any source or storage size.
  2. Site all water infrastructure at least 30 m downhill from latrines, pens, and chemical stores.
  3. Install first-flush diverters on all roof catchment systems.
  4. Line ponds with clay or HDPE; include silt traps and spillways.
  5. Use solar pumps where possible â fuel costs kill smallholder margins.
  6. Cover all tanks and cisterns to prevent evaporation, algae, and mosquito breeding.
  7. Chlorinate wells annually and test water quality before each growing season.
  8. Keep records of water volumes captured and used to track return on investment.

Further Reading

  • FAO â Small-scale irrigation for arid zones: principles and options (free PDF, full technical manual)
  • FAO AQUASTAT â Country-level water resource data for Africa
  • WHO â Guidelines for the Safe Use of Wastewater, Excreta and Greywater in Agriculture (free download)
  • International Water Management Institute (IWMI) â Research on smallholder irrigation in Africa
  • FAO â Irrigation Manual: Planning, Development, Monitoring and Evaluation (free PDF)

Business takeaway: Water storage is not a cost â it is your insurance policy against drought and your license to grow high-value crops year-round. Every dollar invested in reliable, clean water storage returns 3â5 times in avoided crop loss and premium market access. Start small, measure everything, and reinvest your irrigation profits into bigger storage.

quiz.q: What is the ideal depth for a farm pond to prevent it from drying out quickly?
quiz.explanation: A depth of at least 2 meters helps the pond retain water longer during dry periods.

quiz.q: Which soil type is best for a farm pond without a liner?
quiz.explanation: Clay soil holds water well because it has small particles that prevent rapid drainage.

quiz.q: What is the purpose of a silt trap before a pond inlet?
options: B) To settle sand and debris
quiz.explanation: A silt trap allows sand and debris to settle before water enters the pond, reducing mud buildup.

quiz.q: How much water can a 10m x 10m x 2m deep pond hold?
quiz.explanation: Volume = 10 x 10 x 2 = 200 cubic meters, and 1 cubic meter = 1,000 liters, so 200,000 liters.

quiz.q: Why should you keep at least 30 cm of water in a lined pond?
options: B) To protect the liner and seal
D) To make it look nice
quiz.explanation: A minimum water level prevents the liner from drying out and cracking, which would cause leaks.

quiz.q: For rainwater harvesting, what is the formula to calculate potential collection?
options: A) Roof area x rainfall x 0.8
quiz.explanation: The formula accounts for roof area, rainfall depth, and an 80% collection efficiency.

quiz.q: What is a first-flush diverter used for?
options: B) To discard the first dirty rainwater
C) To store the first rain
quiz.explanation: It dumps the initial rainwater that carries dirt, bird droppings, and debris from the roof.

quiz.q: Which material is commonly used for cheap ferrocement tanks?
quiz.explanation: Ferrocement tanks are built with a wire mesh frame plastered with cement-sand mix.

quiz.q: Why should rainwater tanks be covered?
options: B) To prevent mosquitoes and algae
D) To make them look better
quiz.explanation: Covering tanks stops mosquitoes from breeding and reduces algae growth by blocking sunlight.

quiz.q: What is the maximum recommended depth for a shallow well?
quiz.explanation: Shallow wells are typically less than 15 meters deep and rely on a high water table.

quiz.q: What should you do if a hand-dug well keeps collapsing?
options: B) Line the walls with concrete rings or bricks
quiz.explanation: Lining the walls with concrete rings or bricks prevents collapse and makes the well safe.

quiz.q: How often should you check pump seals on a well?
quiz.explanation: Checking seals every 3 months helps prevent leaks and maintains pump efficiency.

quiz.q: What is the purpose of shock-chlorination in a well?
options: D) To lower the water table
quiz.explanation: Shock-chlorination uses bleach to kill bacteria and pathogens in the well.

quiz.q: How much water can a 1 HP pump lift from 10 meters?
quiz.explanation: A 1 HP pump typically moves about 1,000 liters per hour at 10 meters head.

quiz.q: What is the first step before using a stream for irrigation?
quiz.explanation: Measuring flow rate tells you if the stream can supply enough water for your pump.

quiz.q: What is 'head' in pumping terms?
options: B) The total vertical lift plus friction losses
quiz.explanation: Head is the total height the pump must push water, including vertical lift and friction in pipes.

quiz.q: Why should you avoid pumping muddy water?
options: B) It wears out the pump impeller
D) It cools the pump too much
quiz.explanation: Mud and grit in water cause rapid wear on the pump's impeller and seals.

quiz.q: What is a sump in a stream?
options: B) A small hole to collect water
quiz.explanation: A sump is a dug hole in the stream bed that collects water for the pump intake during low flow.

quiz.q: How often should you change the oil in a petrol pump?
quiz.explanation: Changing oil every 50 hours of use keeps the engine lubricated and running smoothly.

quiz.q: Which storage option is best for very large volumes of water?
quiz.explanation: Earth dams can store millions of liters, far more than tanks.

quiz.q: What is a spillway on a dam?
options: B) A channel to release excess water
quiz.explanation: A spillway safely carries excess water around the dam to prevent overtopping and failure.

quiz.q: How can you reduce evaporation from a reservoir?
options: B) Cover with shade net or floating cover
quiz.explanation: A physical cover reduces evaporation by blocking sunlight and wind.

quiz.q: What is the recommended compaction layer thickness for an earth dam?
quiz.explanation: Compacting soil in 20 cm layers ensures a dense, stable dam wall.

quiz.q: Why should you fence a reservoir?
options: A) To keep out animals and people
quiz.explanation: Fencing prevents animals from contaminating water and people from falling in.

quiz.q: How much water can a 5,000-liter tank irrigate for tomatoes?
quiz.explanation: A 5,000-liter tank can supply about 100 tomato plants for two weeks, depending on climate.

quiz.q: What is the minimum distance animals should be kept from a water source?
quiz.explanation: Keeping animals at least 30 meters away reduces the risk of fecal contamination.

quiz.q: What does a first-flush diverter do for rainwater quality?
options: B) Removes the first dirty water
quiz.explanation: It discards the initial rainwater that contains most of the dirt and contaminants from the roof.

quiz.q: How much bleach (5% chlorine) is needed to treat 1,000 liters of water?
quiz.explanation: For large tanks, use 1 liter of bleach per 1,000 liters of water to disinfect.

quiz.q: Why should you compost manure before applying it near water?
options: B) To reduce E. coli and pathogens
C) To make it smell better
quiz.explanation: Composting for at least 6 months kills harmful bacteria like E. coli that can contaminate water.

quiz.q: How often should you clean a water tank?
quiz.explanation: Cleaning every 6 months removes sediment and prevents algae and bacterial growth.
